_comment: THE EDIT, AS DATA. One row per beat, in order.
`audio` is the narration take for that beat. Record one file per beat -
the locked script already says one take per chunk, and this is why: a
fluffed line costs one beat and its visual retimes around it automatically.
`visual` is either a still (png) or a player (html). A still is held for
exactly as long as its audio runs. A player is RE-CAPTURED at the audio's
measured length, so the animation stretches to the narration rather than
the narration being cut to the animation. That is the whole reason the
`live` marks the beats you shoot yourself. assemble.py will use the file
at `visual` if it exists and tell you which ones are still missing.
Paths are relative to the repository root.
`live: true` marks a beat you screen-record yourself. assemble.py accepts
an mp4 there and retimes it to the take like any other visual - a clip
shorter than its narration holds on its last frame rather than cutting

beats.live_alternative: screen recording of the agent, if you shoot it

beats.note: the architecture beat. Retimes to the take, which is what the cue file's own provenance says to do.

beats.how: REAL OUTPUT, RENDERED. Rebuild the transcript and the card with: powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File tools\capture\gcp-proof.ps1 -Pause 0.05 | Out-File -Encoding utf8 tools/capture/out/gcp-proof-transcript.txt ; then python tools/capture/build-terminal-view.py
beats.prefer_live: A SCREEN RECORDING IS STRICTLY BETTER AS PROOF and supersedes this. If you shoot one, drop it at video/N6a-gcp-terminal.mp4 and change this beat's `visual` to that path - assemble.py takes mp4 and fits it to the narration. Nothing else changes.

beats.note: the run view - what that infrastructure produced. Follows the terminal, which established that it is real.
